transcript.text: washing machine making a horrible noise

A horrible noise can range from a simple unbalanced load or a machine rocking on its feet, to something mechanical such as an object caught near the drum, a loose paddle, or worn drum bearings. The sound and when it occurs are the quickest way to separate these. 1. Switch the machine off and unplug it. Press each top corner: it should not rock. If it does, a foot may need adjusting or the floor may be uneven — this commonly causes banging on spin.
2. With the drum empty and the power off, turn the drum slowly by hand. A light metallic tick or scrape suggests a coin, bra wire or similar object; a rough, deep grumble or noticeable looseness when lifting the drum points more towards bearings/support.
3. If the noise was during spin with a duvet, bath mat, one heavy item or a very small load, redistribute it and try an ordinary mixed load. If it is then quiet, it is likely just an imbalance. What sort of noise is it, and when does it happen: violent banging/shaking on spin, a deep rumble/roar as it speeds up, or a metallic tick/scrape as the drum turns? Is it with every normal load or only particular items?
It's a deep rumble/roar when it spins, like a jet engine. Every load now, it's got worse over a few months. Quieter during the wash.

A deep jet-engine roar that is getting progressively worse and is loudest on spin is most often worn drum bearings. A failing drum support (spider) can give similar symptoms; an unlevel machine can add vibration, but would not usually cause a steadily worsening roar on every load. 1. Switch off and unplug the machine. Open the door and turn the empty drum slowly by hand. Roughness, grating or a low rumble supports bearing wear; a smooth, quiet turn makes it less certain.
2. Still unplugged, hold the inner drum at the top and gently lift/rock it. A noticeable clunk, up-and-down movement or the drum sitting low points to bearings or the drum support, rather than a loading problem.
3. Also do the stationary check from before: press each top corner. If the cabinet rocks, level the feet first. That may reduce vibration, but it would not normally cure the roaring noise itself. Avoid repeated high-speed spins while it is this noisy: if the drum develops obvious play, catches the door seal, leaks, or makes a harsh grinding sound, stop using it and arrange an engineer. Bearing/support repairs require substantial dismantling, so they are not usually a basic DIY job.

Turned the drum by hand and it rumbles/grinds. When I lift the edge up and down there's a noticeable clunky up and down play. Can't see any coins or anything in the holes. Is it worth fixing on a 9 year old machine?

On the evidence so far, this is very likely worn drum bearings, with the drum spider/support a lesser possibility. The progressively worsening jet-engine roar, rough grinding by hand and clunky up-and-down drum play are the classic combination. Is it worth fixing at nine years old? Usually only if it is a good-quality machine in otherwise excellent condition and an engineer suggests that the bearings are separately repairable. This is a major strip-down repair, and on many machines the outer tub is sealed, meaning the tub assembly rather than just bearings may be required. In that situation, repair often does not make financial sense on a nine-year-old machine. If the drum spider is damaged as well, replacement is even less attractive. 1. With it switched off and unplugged, look through the door opening. Turn the empty drum slowly: if it sits low/off-centre or catches the door seal, a failed spider/support becomes more likely alongside the bearings.
2. I would avoid further high-speed use. Stop using it altogether if the drum catches the seal, there is a leak, black/oily marks appear on laundry, or the noise becomes harsh grinding. The sensible next step is an engineer’s diagnosis and a fixed repair quote, specifically asking whether the outer tub is repairable and whether the drum spider is sound. If the quote is substantial relative to a replacement, replacement is the more sensible choice at this age.
